whatWeDo.title: What we do
whatWeDo.lead: Three kinds of engagement. Most projects start as one and quietly become another, which is fine — we would rather be useful than tidy.

offerings.name: Build
offerings.lead: New products and platforms, from the first commit to production.
body: Most of what makes software expensive is decided in the first few weeks: the data model, the boundaries between systems, what the team is allowed to assume. We want to be there for that part, and to still be there when it ships.
We work in your repository, in your process, with your people. Not a black box that returns a deliverable and an invoice.
items: Frontend architecture and API surface design

offerings.name: Rescue
offerings.lead: Codebases that became slow, fragile, or that nobody wants to own.
body: We start with an audit and a written verdict: what is actually wrong, what it is costing you, and what we would do about it in which order. Sometimes that document is the entire engagement. More often we stay and do the work.
A rewrite is the last option, not the first. Most systems can be brought back incrementally while they keep serving users, and the ones that genuinely cannot are rarer than people think.
items: Handovers from agencies or departing teams

offerings.name: Lead
offerings.lead: Interim technical leadership for teams that are between people, or growing faster than they can hire.
body: We take responsibility rather than seats: technical direction, architecture decisions, interviewing, review culture, mentoring. The kind of work that does not show up in a sprint report but decides how the next year goes.
The goal is to become unnecessary. We write down what we know and leave the team able to carry it.
items: Interim tech lead and engineering management

closing.text: That is usually a good reason to talk. A first conversation costs nothing and often resolves the question by itself.

howWeWork.title: How we work
howWeWork.lead: Quality is a process, not a promise. This is ours — written down, because principles that are never stated are not principles.

principles.name: We take on few projects at a time
text: Attention does not scale and neither does judgment. Taking on fewer clients is the only reliable method we know for keeping the quality of the work honest.
It also means we sometimes say no, or say later. We would rather do that than quietly give you less than you are paying for.

principles.name: Senior people only
text: Nobody learns on your budget. Everyone who touches your project has shipped this kind of thing before.

When a project needs more hands or another discipline, we bring in people from our network — developers, designers and specialists we have worked with and would work with again. We do not answer a staffing problem by hiring a stranger and hoping.

principles.name: We work in the open
text: In your repository, your tracker, your channels. You can see what is happening on any given day rather than at the end of a sprint.
If something is going badly, you will hear it from us first, and early enough to still do something about it.

principles.name: Agents do volume. We do direction.
text: We use AI agents heavily, and we are precise about where. They are good at breadth: migrations, test coverage, mechanical refactors, boilerplate, the fiftieth variation of a form. They are not good at deciding what should exist.
Architecture, trade-offs and review stay with us. Nothing ships that we cannot explain line by line, and nothing is merged because a machine sounded confident.
The point is not speed for its own sake. It is that a small studio can now hold a quality bar that used to need a large team — which is exactly why we can stay small.

principles.name: Quality is enforced, not intended
text: Types, tests, review and CI. Standards that a tired person on a Friday afternoon still meets, because the pipeline does not let anything else through.
Good intentions are not a quality strategy. Neither is a document nobody reads.

principles.name: We leave things owned
text: Documentation, runbooks, decision records, and a team that can carry on. An engagement that ends with the knowledge walking out of the door has failed, however good the code was.
The best outcome is that you need us less next year than this one.

studio.title: Studio
studio.lead: wiremore is a product engineering studio in Berlin. Independent, deliberately small, and older than most of the tools it works with.

company.label: The company
company.title: Small on purpose.
text: We have been building software for other people’s companies for over a decade, as wiremore GmbH, from Berlin — for clients in Germany, Switzerland and further afield.

We have never wanted to be an agency. Growing headcount changes what a studio is: more of the work becomes managing the work. We would rather stay at the size where the people who talk to you are the people who build the thing.

principal.label: Principal
principal.title: Manuel Bieh
text: wiremore was founded and is run by Manuel Bieh. He has been building for the web for 25 years and has worked with React since its early days.

He wrote <book>React Deep Dive</book> — 320 pages, and the first comprehensive book about React written in German. He has led teams as interim tech lead, worked as architect and developer, and shipped in automotive, regulated finance, media, logistics and health.
More detail, and a full CV, at <site>manuelbieh.de</site>.

network.label: The network
network.title: Around the studio.
text: Around wiremore is a network of senior developers, designers and specialists built up over two decades of working together — people we have shipped with, argued with, and would happily do both with again.

When a project needs another discipline or more hands than the studio has, that is where they come from. It is the reason a small studio can take on work that looks too big for it, and the reason we do not need to grow to say yes.

products.label: Our own products
products.title: We build for ourselves, too.
products.lead: It keeps us honest about what shipping actually costs — deadlines nobody set for us, and no client to blame.

contact.title: Contact
contact.lead: Email is the best way to reach us.
body: Tell us what you are building, roughly when you need it, and what already exists. That is usually enough for a first useful answer rather than a discovery call about having a discovery call.
If it turns out we are not the right studio for the job, we will say so — and where we can, point you at someone who is.
contact.phoneNote: We do not list a phone number. Email gets a faster answer, and it gives us something to think about before we reply.
